ch03.card: Part 2 of 8. The reader: giving every letter a meaning.
ch03.s01.c1: The question goes to the reader first. The reader is a borrowed model called Gemma, and it reads the whole question one time.
ch03.s01.c2: Think of a translator who already knows English well. That is a picture only. We borrowed him, and we cannot change him. He lent us his skills.
ch03.s02.c1: Gemma cuts text into word pieces, called tokens. Where the cuts fall in Tom has 12 apples is a made-up example, a picture only.
ch03.s02.c2: Our thinker, the part that does the thinking, works on letters. It has one spot for each letter, not for each word piece.
ch03.s03.c1: On 20,000 of our skill questions, one token covers 3.08 letters on average. We measured that by count.
ch03.s03.c2: On 9,068 web-text chunks of 279 letters, one token covers 4.27 letters on average.
ch03.s04.c1: Gemma reads the whole question one time. After that, it does not read the question again.
ch03.s04.c2: Each token gets a row of 768 numbers that holds its meaning in context.
ch03.s04.c3: Each letter takes the row of the token it sits in. So letters in a token share its meaning.
ch03.s05.c1: The reader holds 271,002,624 numbers, all set before our work began.
ch03.s05.c2: About 134 million are a word table, one row per word piece. About 137 million are reading layers, plus a step widening rows to 768.
ch03.s05.c3: It is frozen: our practice never changes it. Its own reading limit is 8,192 tokens, which is not our limit.
ch03.s06.c1: One linear layer, a learned mix of numbers, turns Gemma's 768 numbers into the thinker's row length, its width.
ch03.s06.c2: At width 256 it has about 197 thousand learned numbers. At width 512 it has about 394 thousand.
ch03.s07.c1: First: which letter it is. A learned row of numbers. It is like a note card with a row of numbers.
ch03.s07.c2: Second: where it sits in the question. A learned table with 2,000 rows in the planned finished design, B3, and 280 in the growth test, G1.
ch03.s07.c3: Third: how far its letter sits from the end of its word. The count is hand-written, but the row it picks is learned.
ch03.s07.c4: Fourth: Gemma's meaning, through the converter plug, is added on top. Then the letter window reads the sum.
ch03.s08.c1: Two small learned layers read the summed row. They are ours, not borrowed. Ours means our practice sets them.
ch03.s08.c2: Each layer looks 2 letters left and 2 right, so together a letter sees 4 letters each side. It sees its neighbours.
ch03.s08.c3: The window adds about 0.7 million numbers at width 256, and about 2.6 million at 512.
ch03.s09.c1: Letter-cipher puzzles are one kind of test question. Each copy, a separate training run, gets 40 familiar-style ones, scored out of 100.
ch03.s09.c2: With the window, Gemma plus letters scores 97.5 and 95.0 on two copies.
ch03.s09.c3: Without it, Gemma plus letters scores 5.0 and 2.5.
ch03.s09.c4: Letters alone, without it, score 12.5 and 2.5. This was tested on only two copies, and on one kind of question.
ch03.s10.c1: The position table has one row per spot, so it sets the longest question. That is 280 letters in the growth test, G1, and 2,000 in planned B3. Letters past that limit would have no spot.
ch03.s10.c2: In a sample of 4,000 bAbI test questions, a public set of story puzzles, 32% run over 280 letters and 1% over 2,000.
ch03.s11.c1: A plain pattern, written by hand, finds the numbers in the question. It is ordinary code.
ch03.s11.c2: It records where each number is, not its value.
ch03.s11.c3: Room to mark: 16 numbers in the calculator-outside model, T1SDR, 91 in the growth test, G1, and 240 in planned B3.
ch03.s12.c1: In B3, the plain-code calculator's reply, shown as sub 12, 5 equals 7, is read by the letter window.
ch03.s12.c2: Gemma does not read replies. It read the question once.
ch03.s12.c3: Suggested reasoning, and untested: a reply carries nothing Gemma would add.
ch03.s13.c1: On 6,040 test questions kept aside, five kinds called Pooled-5, six separate training runs, or copies, with the reader scored 75.9 to 77.2.
ch03.s13.c2: Eight copies of the same model without the reader scored 73.0 to 74.7.
ch03.s13.c3: On average the reader is ahead by 2.67 points out of 100, in all 6 copies, at 3M, about 3 million learned numbers.
ch03.s14.c1: A leak means some answers are right with zero rounds of thinking.
ch03.s14.c2: Averaged over 6 copies, the zero-round leak is 6.59. The pass mark, set in advance as the no-reader average plus 1.0, was 4.62. Missed.
ch03.s14.c3: On seed 200, on familiar questions, the reader version scored 18.09 with zero rounds. The same model without it scored 1.40.
ch03.s14.c4: Copies without the reader leak on some seeds too, so the cause is not settled.
ch03.s15.c1: A test called TK would let the thinker read one spot per token, or word piece, instead of one per letter.
ch03.s15.c2: The code and a PC job file exist, but it has never been run, so there is no result. Letters or tokens is still undecided.
ch03.s16.c1: The reader is borrowed and frozen. It reads the question once. Borrowed means someone else trained it.
ch03.s16.c2: Each letter gets a meaning in context, plus a window of 4 letters each side.
ch03.s16.c3: Without the window, the Gemma version scored 5.0 and 2.5 out of 100 on cipher puzzles, in two copies.
